title: Emerging Markets Learn a Painful Lesson as AI Tech Hype Unravels
excerpt: South Korea's KOSPI lost 40% in six weeks and volatility surpassed COVID-era peaks as AI-fueled concentration turned once-diversified emerging market indexes into ground zero for the global tech selloff.
body:
• South Korea's KOSPI index lost 40% in six weeks after doubling on AI-driven gains, with emerging market volatility surpassing COVID-era peaks.
  • Nine companies — mostly Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers plus Alibaba and Tencent — now account for over 40% of the MSCI Emerging Markets index, making it more concentrated than U.S. benchmarks.
  • India has emerged as the "anti-AI" trade, with foreign investors rotating $1.7 billion into Indian equities in July as they exited crowded AI positions in South Korea and Taiwan.

A few years ago, veteran emerging market fund manager Carlos von Hardenberg struggled to get investors interested in anything outside U.S. tech stocks. The AI boom changed that — and now he's watching those same investors scramble for cover.

The artificial intelligence frenzy that lit a rocket under South Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers has turned into a cautionary tale about concentration risk. South Korea's KOSPI index, which had doubled in value on the back of massive gains for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, ripped back 40% in just six weeks starting in late June. Taiwan's TSMC, the largest company in the emerging market stock universe, fell nearly 14%.

Volatility Beyond COVID Peaks

The selloff sent volatility in South Korean markets skyrocketing. Even for MSCI's $1.8 trillion emerging market benchmark — encompassing more than 1,175 companies from 24 countries — volatility surpassed the peaks of the COVID pandemic, according to MSCI data.

"The clients that we speak to, the institutional clients, are struggling with the level of volatility in Korea at the moment. To the point that they think that any sort of fundamental positive earnings story that may exist is not worth pursuing at this point."

— William Bratton, Head of Cash Equity Research for APAC, BNP Paribas

The Korean market's swings have been larger than bitcoin's this year, while the recent rout produced the most dramatic drop in the MSCI EM index's "liquidity factor" ever recorded — a sign of investors fleeing the shares that had been surging.

Just nine companies — mostly the big Taiwanese and Korean tech firms, plus Alibaba and Tencent in China — now account for more than 40% of the MSCI EM index, making it even more top-heavy than the U.S. S&P 500.

A Classic Case of 'Careful What You Wish For'

"What we're seeing is that emerging markets, which people used to look to as a source of diversification, because of the emergence and importance of these extremely large AI-related companies, are not really a source of diversification anymore," said MSCI's research head Ashley Lester. "They're right in the centre of the AI boom."

International investors pulled money out of Asia-excluding-China share markets faster than during any six-month period going back to at least 2010, according to LSEG data. South Korea and Taiwan bore the brunt, shedding over $100 billion and $44 billion respectively, according to JPMorgan, as fund concentration rules forced investors to cash in some of the 500% and 1,100% twelve-month gains on Samsung and SK Hynix.

India: The Unlikely Beneficiary

One country's misfortune has become another's opportunity. India, whose lack of direct AI exposure made it an underperformer for much of 2025 and early 2026, is now attracting investors fleeing the volatility.

India's benchmark Sensex climbed 5% since mid-June even as South Korean and Taiwanese markets tumbled. Indian IT stocks have been the biggest beneficiaries, with the Nifty IT index surging 16.7% in July as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped 21% — the widest margin of outperformance for any month since 1999, according to Goldman Sachs.

"India has emerged as the obvious destination for investors trimming their exposure to North Asian and U.S. technology stocks," said Todd McClone, a portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management, which oversees about $65 billion.

Several major banks have upgraded India in recent weeks. HSBC moved India to "neutral" from "underweight," UBS lifted its rating to "attractive," and Goldman Sachs and Bernstein have flagged the prospect of a second-half Nifty rebound.

Navigating the Storm

Not everyone is heading for the exits. Ji Young Park, a portfolio manager at Amundi, Europe's biggest fund manager, said she had started scaling back exposure before the turbulence but the selloff was still costly. "I think in the last month there have been six or seven circuit breakers on the Korean stock market, so it tells you just how volatile it has been," Park said.

UBP technology portfolio manager Dimitri Kallianiotis advised clients not to panic. "Ride the volatility and try to avoid the overhyped names," he said. "If you are not invested in the tempest days, you won't be there for the rebound."

For investors in the Indian diaspora with exposure to both Indian and global emerging markets, the lesson is clear: concentration cuts both ways. The AI trade that bypassed India is now sending capital back, but the broader emerging market reckoning is far from over.
image_caption: Samsung Electronics, a bellwether for Asian tech markets, has seen its stock slide amid weakening AI chip demand and rising geopolitical uncertainty.
nri_angle: India is emerging as an unlikely beneficiary of the AI selloff, with foreign investors rotating back into Indian equities after months of outflows, making the country's 'anti-AI' trade status a potential advantage for diaspora investors.
author: Diaspora Desk
